exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Derives the sensor-bias contribution from tanh Lipschitz continuity, unrolls the ultimate bound and independently checks invariance and actuator range.
exercises.replacement_html:
1. Include the biased controller measurement. The normalized temperature update is $e_{t+1}=0.9e_t-0.3\tanh(e_t+b_t)+w_t$, with $|b_t|\le0.03$ and $|w_t|\le0.02$. Write the nominal closed-loop map as $F(e)=0.9e-0.3\tanh e$. Its derivative is $0.9-0.3(1-\tanh^2e)$, between $0.6$ and $0.9$, and $F(0)=0$. The mean value theorem gives $|F(e)|\le0.9|e|$.

Because $\tanh$ is 1-Lipschitz, $|\tanh(e+b)-\tanh e|\le|b|$. The extra next-error contribution is therefore at most $0.3(0.03)=0.009$. Adding the disturbance gives

$$|e_{t+1}|\le0.9|e_t|+0.009+0.02=0.9|e_t|+0.029.$$

2. Derive the ultimate bound. Repeating the inequality gives $|e_t|\le0.9^t|e_0|+0.029\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}0.9^j=0.9^t|e_0|+0.29(1-0.9^t)$. Hence $\limsup_t|e_t|\le0.29$, corresponding to $2.9$ degrees because the normalization is ten degrees per unit.

3. Check the whole operating interval. If $|e_t|\le0.5$, then $|e_{t+1}|\le0.9(0.5)+0.029=0.479\le0.5$. This proves invariance by induction under every allowed bias and disturbance sequence.

4. Check the actuator separately. The measured normalized error has $|e_t+b_t|\le0.53$. Oddness and monotonicity of tanh give $|u_t|=1.5|\tanh(e_t+b_t)|\le1.5\tanh(0.53)\approx0.728072$ kilowatts, below the $0.8$ kilowatt limit. Persistent bias need not allow zero tracking error; the justified conclusion is this revised ultimate bound and invariant interval.

exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Forms the characteristic polynomial and complex roots, derives their modulus and gives an allowed initial memory state violating invariance despite a feasible command.
exercises.replacement_html:
1. Include controller memory in the state. With $z_t=(e_t,e_{t-1})^\top$, the delayed linear loop is $z_{t+1}=A_dz_t$, where $A_d=\begin{bmatrix}0.9&-0.3\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$. Its characteristic polynomial is $\det(\lambda I-A_d)=\lambda(\lambda-0.9)+0.3=\lambda^2-0.9\lambda+0.3$.

2. Check asymptotic stability. The discriminant is $0.9^2-4(0.3)=0.81-1.2=-0.39$. Thus the roots are $0.45\pm i\sqrt{39}/20\approx0.45\pm0.312250i$. Their squared magnitude is $0.45^2+39/400=0.2025+0.0975=0.3$, so both have magnitude $\sqrt{0.3}\approx0.547723\lt1$. A finite linear discrete-time system with all eigenvalues strictly inside the unit circle has $A_d^t\to0$, hence every augmented trajectory converges to zero.

3. Test containment independently of convergence. The initialization model permits $z_0=(0.5,-0.5)$ in the square. Its next current error is $e_1=0.9(0.5)-0.3(-0.5)=0.45+0.15=0.6\gt0.5$, so the square is not invariant. The initial command is $u_0=-1.5(-0.5)=0.75$ kilowatts, within the $0.8$ limit; saturation is not responsible.

No actuator-bounded prehistory needs to produce this initialized memory pair under the question's assumptions. Stability guarantees eventual convergence, while invariance requires every next state to remain in the permitted set. A delay-aware safety design needs an invariant region in both coordinates whose projection respects the physical temperature limit.

exercises.replacement_html:
1. Read the ellipsoid and rescale it. The inequality is $4x_1^2+x_2^2\le1$, giving semi-axis lengths $1/2$ and $1$. Put $u=(2x_1,x_2)$ so $\|u\|_2\le1$. The pre-activation becomes $v=2x_1+x_2=u_1+u_2$.

2. Bound the linear functional and attain the bound. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|u_1+u_2|\le\|(1,1)\|_2\|u\|_2\le\sqrt2$. At $u=(1,1)/\sqrt2$, the state is $x=(1/(2\sqrt2),1/\sqrt2)$. Its quadratic value is $1/2+1/2=1$, and $v=1/\sqrt2+1/\sqrt2=\sqrt2$. Negating the state attains $-\sqrt2$, so the maximum absolute value is exactly $\sqrt2$.

3. Compare with the proposed local box. Since $\sqrt2\gt1$, the interval $[-1,1]$ omits an actually attainable pre-activation on the ellipsoid. A sector valid only for $|v|\le1$ therefore cannot be used over the whole ellipsoid. Its required half-width is at least $\sqrt2$, consistent with $\sqrt{aP^{-1}a^\top}$ for $a=(2,1)$.

exercises.replacement_html:
(a) Assemble the affine network in its evaluation order. Let the output dimension be $n_u$, so $W_0$ is $n_1$ by $n_x$, $W_1$ is $n_2$ by $n_1$ and $W_2$ is $n_u$ by $n_2$. With $v=(v^1,v^2)$ and $w=(w^1,w^2)$, the three equations are

$$\begin{bmatrix}u\\v^1\\v^2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&W_2&b_2\\W_0&0&0&b_0\\0&W_1&0&b_1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\w^1\\w^2\\1\end{bmatrix}.$$

Reading the block columns gives $N_{ux}=0$, $N_{uw}=[0\ W_2]$, $N_{vx}=[W_0^\top\ 0]^\top$, $N_{vw}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\W_1&0\end{bmatrix}$, $N_{ub}=b_2$, and $N_{vb}=(b_0,b_1)$. Substitution into the plant gives $x^+=Ax+BW_2w^2+Bb_2$.

(b) Establish well-posedness constructively. Given $x$, compute $v^1=W_0x+b_0$, then $w^1=\phi(v^1)$, then $v^2=W_1w^1+b_1$, then $w^2=\phi(v^2)$ and finally $u$. Every quantity depends only on previously computed quantities. Thus the strictly block-lower-triangular $N_{vw}$ creates no algebraic loop; a single-valued activation gives one network output.

(c) Remove biases and map the lifted vector. Set $\zeta=(x,w^1,w^2)$, of length $N=n_x+n_1+n_2$. The required maps satisfy $R_V\zeta=(x,u)$ and $R_\phi\zeta=(v^1,v^2,w^1,w^2)$:

$$R_V=\begin{bmatrix}I&0&0\\0&0&W_2\end{bmatrix},\qquad R_\phi=\begin{bmatrix}W_0&0&0\\0&W_1&0\\0&I&0\\0&0&I\end{bmatrix}.$$

Their column count is $N$; their row counts are $n_x+n_u$ and $2(n_1+n_2)$. Consequently the lifted stability LMI is an $N$ by $N$ symmetric matrix. A symmetric $P$ has $n_x(n_x+1)/2$ free entries, and a diagonal activation multiplier has $n_1+n_2$ entries. Their total is $n_x(n_x+1)/2+n_1+n_2$. The theorem's first-layer local containment conditions add $n_1$ LMIs, each of size $1+n_x$.

(d) Track the changes rather than reusing the origin blindly. For output feedback $u=\pi(Cx)$, replace $W_0$ by $W_0C$. With nonzero biases first solve $x_*=Ax_*+B\pi(x_*)$. Subtracting this equilibrium removes the constant bias column from the difference equations, but the shifted activation of neuron $i$ is $\tilde\varphi_i(s)=\varphi(s+v_{*,i})-\varphi(v_{*,i})$. These maps vanish at zero and require their own valid offset sector bounds. Different equilibrium shifts need not define an identical repeated function, so cross-channel multipliers relying on repetition need an additional shared-shift/common-bound justification.

exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Proves global and local tanh bounds using the mean-value theorem and a differentiated ratio, verifies tight endpoints and compares both numerical boxes and theorem roles.
Derives the full global multiplier interval, verifies an explicit local multiplier analytically, proves the exact attraction interval and provides actual scalar-iteration checkpoints.
exercises.replacement_html:
(a) Apply the global scalar test. Here $g=bW_1=-0.6$ and $c=gW_0=-1.2$. For $a=0.8$, both $|a|=0.8\lt1$ and $|a+c|=0.4\lt1$, so Step 5 permits a strict certificate. With $p=1$, its optimizing multiplier is $\lambda^\star=(1-a^2-ac)/4=(1-0.64+0.96)/4=0.33$. The matrix is

$$\mathcal M(1,0.33)=\begin{bmatrix}a^2-1&ag+2\lambda^\star\\ag+2\lambda^\star&g^2-2\lambda^\star\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.36&0.18\\0.18&-0.30\end{bmatrix}.$$

Its trace is $-0.66$ and determinant is $0.108-0.0324=0.0756$. The symmetric two-by-two eigenvalue formula gives $(-33\pm3\sqrt{37})/100\approx-0.147517,-0.512483$, both negative. For a general multiplier the determinant is $-4\lambda^2+2.64\lambda-0.36$. Its roots are $(33\pm3\sqrt{21})/100$. Because the leading diagonal remains negative, the full admissible set for $p=1$ is the open interval between those roots, approximately $(0.192523,0.467477)$. The endpoints have zero determinant and do not give a strict LMI.

(b) Show the global obstruction and construct the local certificates. For $a=1.3$, the global matrix's leading diagonal is $(1.3^2-1)p=0.69p\gt0$ for every $p\gt0$, which is incompatible with negative definiteness. The linearization is nevertheless $a+c=0.1$, so local stability is possible.

On a pre-activation box $|v|\le d$, let $\alpha=\tanh(d)/d$ for $d\gt0$. The ratio decreases continuously from $1$ to $0$, as proved in Exercise 14.2. Hence there is one positive $r$ with $\tanh(r)/r=1/4$; it satisfies $3.9973\lt r\lt3.9974$. For any $0\lt d\lt r$, $1/4\lt\alpha\lt1$. Choose $p=4/d^2$ and $\lambda=3p/[10(1-\alpha)]$. Substitution into the local-sector LMI gives

$$\mathcal M_\alpha=\frac{p}{1-\alpha}\begin{bmatrix}(69-309\alpha)/100&(-18+138\alpha)/100\\(-18+138\alpha)/100&(-24-36\alpha)/100\end{bmatrix},\qquad \det\mathcal M_\alpha=\frac{99p^2(4\alpha-1)}{500(1-\alpha)}.$$

The leading diagonal is negative for $\alpha\gt1/4$, and the determinant is positive. Thus the local LMI is strictly negative definite. The sublevel $px^2\le1$ is $|x|\le d/2$, which implies $|v|=|2x|\le d$ and verifies containment. Every such closed interval is certified, so their union is $|x_0|\lt r/2$.

Why this union is the exact attraction interval. The true map $F(x)=1.3x-0.6\tanh(2x)$ is odd and strictly increasing, since $F'(x)=1.3-1.2(1-\tanh^2(2x))\ge0.1$. For $0\lt x\lt r/2$, $\tanh(2x)/(2x)\gt1/4$ gives $0\lt F(x)\lt x$. The iterates therefore decrease to a nonnegative fixed point; the only one below $r/2$ is zero, so they converge to zero. At $x=r/2$, $F(x)=x$, giving a nonzero fixed point. Above it, $F(x)\gt x$, and an increasing trajectory cannot have a finite limit because there is no fixed point there. Oddness gives the corresponding negative cases. Thus the supremal radius $r/2\approx1.9987$ is not attained by a strict closed-box certificate.

Numerical checks of representative trajectories. Repeated substitution of the displayed scalar map gives the rounded values below. They illustrate the analytic proof; they do not replace it.

$x_0$$x_{10}$$x_{50}$$x_{100}$
$1.9985$$1.996591$$8.616\cdot10^{-15}$$8.616\cdot10^{-65}$
$1.999$$2.003399$$169.805116$$8.356\cdot10^7$

(c) Give a simple explicit certificate for $d=3$. Keep $\alpha=\tanh(3)/3$ exact. It obeys $0.33\lt\alpha\lt1/3$; the lower bound follows from $e^6\gt199$ in the formula $\tanh3=(e^6-1)/(e^6+1)$. With $(p,\lambda)=(1,1/2)$, the local matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}0.69-4\alpha&0.22+\alpha\\0.22+\alpha&-0.64\end{bmatrix}$. Its leading entry is less than $-0.63$, and its determinant is $-0.49+2.12\alpha-\alpha^2\gt0.1007$, since this polynomial is increasing on $[0.33,1/3]$. Thus it is strictly negative definite.

Rescale both variables by $4/9$ to obtain $(p,\lambda)=(4/9,2/9)$ without changing definiteness. The containment matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}9&2\\2&4/9\end{bmatrix}$, with positive diagonal and determinant $4-4=0$, so it is PSD. This certifies the closed interval $|x|\le1/\sqrt p=1.5$, whose pre-activation satisfies $|2x|\le3$.

exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Separates current-sector decrease from next-state membership, works the specified box/ellipse counterexample and gives the noncircular containment induction.
Derives both equilibrium offset equations and a reproducible root solve, then computes the augmented characteristic polynomials and qualifies the local convergence certificate.
exercises.replacement_html:
(a) Solve the true equilibrium equation. Put $e=x_\infty-r$ and use $a=0.5$. With nominal $b=1$ and disturbance $d=0.1$, substituting the controller into $x_\infty=ax_\infty+b\kappa(x_\infty,r)+d$ and cancelling the nominal reference terms gives $0.5e+0.3\tanh e=0.1$. With true $b=1.2$ and $d=0$, the same substitution gives $0.5(r+e)=1.2[0.5r-0.3\tanh e]$, or $0.5e+0.36\tanh e=0.1r$.

For $r=1$, each left-hand side is strictly increasing, with derivative $0.5+q(1-\tanh^2e)\gt0$ for $q=0.3$ or $0.36$, so there is a unique root. Newton's scalar update is $e^+=e-[0.5e+q\tanh e-0.1]/[0.5+q(1-\tanh^2e)]$. Starting from the linearized estimates $0.1/(0.5+q)$ gives respectively $e\approx0.125244$ and $e\approx0.116498$. Thus the output settles at approximately $1.125244$ or $1.116498$, rather than $1$.

The corresponding true state map has derivative $a-0.3b(1-\tanh^2(x-r))$, in $[0.2,0.5]$ for $b=1$ and $[0.14,0.5]$ for $b=1.2$. Both are global contractions, proving convergence to these unique equilibria. A controller's steady-state identity for the nominal plant does not force the same identity for a changed plant.

(b) Use integration to impose the steady-state condition. At an equilibrium of $\xi^+=\xi+r-y$, equality $\xi^+=\xi$ forces $y=r$. For $b\ne0$ and $k_\xi=0.2$, the required equilibrium exists at $x=r$ with $\xi=[(1-a)r-b\kappa(r,r)-d]/(bk_\xi)$. For example, $b=1.2,d=0.1,r=1$ gives $\xi=(0.5-0.6-0.1)/0.24=-5/6$.

Linearizing in deviations of $(x,\xi)$ at that equilibrium gives $A_\xi=\begin{bmatrix}a-0.3b&0.2b\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}$. For $b=1$, its characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2-1.2\lambda+0.4$, with roots $0.6\pm0.2i$ of magnitude $\sqrt{0.4}$. For $b=1.2$, it is $\lambda^2-1.14\lambda+0.38$, whose roots are a complex conjugate pair of magnitude $\sqrt{0.38}$. Both magnitudes are below one. The continuously differentiable closed loop is therefore locally exponentially stable at the equilibrium; this local linearization does not guarantee convergence from arbitrary initial augmented states.

(c) State what the full certificate must add. It must prove convergence of the actual augmented loop on the claimed initial-state/reference set: all references, one reference or a stated reference family according to the theorem used. Persistent disturbances and changed gains must be included in the model covered by that stability certificate. Once the true loop converges to an equilibrium, the integrator structurally forces zero output offset; no separate nominal network steady-state matching condition is needed. Offset-freeness alone does not establish convergence or the size of a region of attraction.
